Title: The nearest neighbor interchange proximity measure for the tree-basedness of rooted binary phylogenetic networks

URL Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23426v1

Published Time: Mon, 19 Oct 2026 01:16:19 GMT

Number of Pages: 20

Markdown Content:
# The nearest neighbor interchange proximity measure for the tree-basedness of rooted binary phylogenetic networks 

## Martin Frohn 1,* and Takatora Suzuki 2

> 1

## Department of Advanced Computing Sciences, Maastricht University, Maastricht, 6229 EN, The Netherlands 

> 2

## Department of Applied Mathematics, Faculty of Fundamental Science and Engineering, Waseda University, Japan 

> *

## Corresponding Author. Email: martin.frohn@maastrichtuniversity.nl 

## Abstract. Tree-based networks are a broad graph class in phylogenetics which posit a model of evolution composed of tree-like processes and hybridization events. Hence, for any non-tree-based phylogenetic network, it is meaningful to study the magnitude of violation of the tree-based model assumptions. For rooted networks, we introduce the proximity measure δrNNI , defined by the minimum number of rooted nearest neighbor interchanges (NNIs) required to transform a network into a tree-based network. For binary networks, we prove that δrNNI is pairwise distinct from all previously known proximity measures in the literature and that no approximation guarantees between δrNNI and other known proximity measures holds. In addition, we characterize a family of networks for which a linear time lower bound on δrNNI is tight. Moreover, we analyze upper bounds and give an exact solution algorithm to compute δrNNI .

## Keywords. Tree-based phylogenetic network, proximity measure, nearest neighbor interchange 

# 1 Introduction 

## Directed weighted acyclic graphs which model evolutionary histories of a set of species are called phylogenetic networks if the leaves are bijectively labeled with the set of species. In the study of evolutionary relationships species are called taxa and it is oftentimes assumed that phylogenetic networks are rooted , i.e., a unique vertex has no parents and is called the root of the network. The evolutionary model constituted by a phylogenetic network that is a tree whose internal vertices have at least degree three is also called a phylogenetic tree .The fundamental class of tree-based phylogenetic networks N generalizes the notion of phylogenetic trees by requiring N to contain a tree T on the same set of taxa and with the same root as N (if it exists), called the 

## support tree of N , such that T has the same vertex set as N [15 ]. Notice that a support tree does not adhere to any degree requirements on vertices like phylogenetic trees. Tree-based networks appear to form a proper generalization of phylogenetic trees by allowing for biological phenomena like horizontal gene transfer and incomplete lineage sorting which are absent from any phylogenetic tree model [1]. However, using them as a model of evolution can exclude biological processes which are inherently not tree-like [3, 5 ]. Consequently, the question arises to which degree a phylogenetic network has a tree-based graph structure. The proximity of a phylogenetic networks to being tree-based can be measured in many different ways. For example by counting the number of vertices deleted from or added to a network to make it tree-based [8],by counting the number of deleted or added edges to make a network tree-based or by modifying it with topological rearrangement moves [6]. Connections between these different proximity measures and algorithms to compute them are typically derived from characterizations of tree-based phylogenetic networks. Specifically, the tree-based property is related to more general, well-known notions in graph theory such as bipartite matchings [24 ] and vertex-disjoint path partitions [8].In this article, we study nearest neighbor interchanges (NNIs) as a proximity measure δrNNI of tree-basedness for rooted binary phylogenetic networks. To the best of our knowledge a NNI proximity measure for rooted phylogenetic network has not been studied before while the unrooted version has recevied some attention in the literature [6]. We show that all known tree-basedness proximity measures for rooted phylogenetic networks from the literature do guarantee only a linear approximation of δrNNI . To prove this distinguishing feature of δrNNI we leverage the characterization of rooted binary phylogenetic networks N as a partition of zig-zag-paths [10 ]. Furthermore, we introduce lower and upper bounds on δrNNI by extending Theorems 11 and 19 in [20 ] and we analyse the families of networks on which these bounds are tight and not tight. 1arXiv:2610.23426v1 [q-bio.PE] 16 Oct 2026 In Section 2 we introduce notation to formalize the measure δrNNI and provide background information on tree-basedness proximity measures. In Section 3 we show that δrNNI is pairwise distinct from the known tree-basedness proximity measures for binary rooted phylogenetic networks and we discuss an algorithm to compute δrNNI . In Section 4 we give a conclusion and future research directions. 

# 2 Preliminaries on phylogenetic networks and tree-basedness proxim-ity measures 

## In this section we consider various preliminaries which we will use throughout this article. 

## 2.1 Graph theoretical terminology 

## Throughout this paper, we assume that the graphs are finite, directed, simple, and acyclic, unless otherwise stated. For a graph G we denote V (G) and E(G) as the vertex set and edge set of G, respectively. For two graphs G and H, G is a subgraph of H if both V (G) ⊆ V (H) and E(G) ⊆ E(H) hold, in which case we write 

## G ⊆ H. Two directed graphs G and H are said to be isomorphic if there exists a bijection between V (G) and 

## V (H) that yields a bijection between E(G) and E(H). In other words, G and H are isomorphic if there exists a labelling map f : V (G) → V (H) so that there is a one-to-one correspondence between V (G) and V (H) and for any vi and vj in V (G), (vi , vj ) is in E(G) if and only if ( f (vi ), f (vj )) is in E(H), including the loops and parallel edges if they exist. A subgraph G of H is proper if G̸ = H.Given a graph G and a non-empty subset S ⊆ E(G), the edge-set S is said to induce the subgraph G [S] of G ,that is, the one whose edge-set is S and whose vertex-set is the set of the ends of all edges in S. For a graph G

## with |E(G)| ≥ 1 and a partition {E1, . . . , Ed } of E(G), the collection {G[E1], . . . , G[Ed ]} is a decomposition of G,and G is said to be decomposed into {G[E1], . . . , G[Ed ]}.For an edge e = ( u, v) of a graph G, u and v are denoted by tail (e) and head (e), respectively. For a graph G

## and v ∈ V (G), we denote din (v) and dout (v) as the number of edges e of G with head (e) = v and tail (e) = v,respectively. We call G binary and almost-binary if din (v) + dout (v) ≤ 3 and din (v) + dout (v) ≤ 4, respectively, for all v ∈ V (G). For an edge (u, v) of a directed graph G, subdividing edge (u, v) refers to the operation of introducing a new vertex p and replacing (u, v) with the new consecutive edges (u, p) and (p, v). Conversely, for a vertex p ∈ V (G) with din (p) = dout (p) = 1, we call p an edge subdivision of G. Similarly, subdividing an edge {u, v} of an undirected graph G refers to the replacement of {u, v} by two edges {u, p}, {p, v} for a new vertex p, and a edge subdivision p ∈ V (G) is defined by deg (p) = 2. Two directed graphs G and H are said to be (graph) isomorphic if there exists a bijection between V (G)

## and V (H) that yields a bijection between E(G) and E(H). In other words, G and H are isomorphic if there exists a labelling map f : V (G) → V (H) so that there is a one-to-one correspondence between V (G) and V (H)

## and for any vi and vj in V (G), (vi , vj ) is in E(G) if and only if ( f (vi ), f (vj )) is in E(H), including the loops and parallel edges if they exist. 

## 2.2 Phylogenetic networks 

## We complete the definition of a phylogenetic network N from the introduction by requiring that the underlying directed weighted acyclic graph of N contains no edge subdivisions. Since edge lengths and the bijection between leaves and species are not a focal point in this article we refer to phylogenetic networks as their underlying graphs if not explicitly stated otherwise. If a phylogenetic network N is rooted, then we denote the unique root of N by ρ(N ). By definition din (ρ(N )) = 0 and there exists a directed path from ρ(G) to any vertex 

## v with din (v) = 1 and dout (v) = 0, called a leaf of N . For a rooted phylogenetic network N , we call v ∈ V (N ) a

## reticulation vertex if din (v) ≥ 2 and dout (v) = 1, a internal tree vertex if din (v) = 1 and dout (v) ≥ 2 and a leaf if 

## din (v) = 1 and dout (v) = 0. Notice that every unrooted binary phylogenetic network can be transformed into a rooted binary phylogenetic network and vice versa by deleting one edge incident to a leaf and orienting edges with respect to the binary constraint or attaching a new leaf to the root and removing edge orientations. For a phylogenetic network N = ( V, E), a covering subtree of N is a subtree of N with the same leaf-set and root. Recall that a covering subtree T of N is called a support tree of N if V (T ) = V (N ) holds, and a phylogenetic network N is called tree-based if there exists a support tree of N . For simplicity of notation, we denote the set of rooted binary phylogenetic networks by N and the set of rooted binary tree-based phylogenetic networks by NTB .Next, we review definitions from [10, 20 ] who are relevant to our study. Given a rooted almost-binary phylogenetic network N , a connected subgraph Z of N with m := |E(Z)| ≥ 1 is a zig-zag trail (in N ) if the 2edges of Z can be permuted as (e1, . . . , em) such that either head (ei ) = head (ei+1) or tail (ei ) = tail (ei+1) holds for each i ∈ [1, m − 1]. A zig-zag trail is represented by an alternating sequence of (not necessarily distinct) vertices and distinct edges, e.g., (v0, (v0, v1), v1, (v2, v1), v2, . . . , (vm, vm−1), vm), but this can be more concisely written as v0 > v1 < v2 > · · · > vm−1 < vm or its reverse, where each edge (vi , vi+1) is represented by vi > vi+1.A zig-zag trail Z in N is maximal if N contains no zig-zag trail Z′ such that Z is a proper subgraph of Z′. Each maximal zig-zag trail in N falls into one of the following four types. A crown is a maximal zig-zag trail Z that has even m := |E(Z)| ≥ 4 and can be written in the cyclic form v0 < v1 > v2 < v3 > · · · > vm−2 < vm−1 > vm = v0.A fence is any maximal zig-zag trail that is not a crown. An N-fence is a fence Z with odd m := |E(Z)| ≥ 1, expressed as v0 > v1 < v2 > · · · < vm−1 > vm. A fence Z with even m := |E(Z)| ≥ 2 is an M-fence if expressed as v0 < v1 > v2 < · · · < vm−1 > vm, and it is a W-fence if expressed as v0 > v1 < v2 > · · · > vm−1 < vm. We will make use of these various types of zig-zag trails because they characterize rooted binary phylogenetic networks: 

## Theorem 2.1. [10 ] Let N ∈ N . Then, there exists a unique decomposition of N into maximal zig-zag trails. 

## We denote the decomposition of N ∈ N into maximal zig-zag trails by Z(N ). Furthermore, maximal zig-zag trails provide a certificate of tree-basedness which has been proven in different contexts: 

## Theorem 2.2. [24, 10, 14 ] Let N ∈ N . Then, N is tree-based if and only if Z(N ) contains no W-fence. 

## 2.3 A review of known tree-basedness proximity measures on rooted phylogenetic networks 

## The following proximity measures of tree-basedness are well-known [8, 22 ]:

## Problem 2.3. Given a rooted phylogenetic network N , calculate the minimum number of 1. leaves in a rooted spanning tree of N which are not leaves in N ;2. vertex disjoint paths that partition V (N ) minus the number of leaves in N ;3. leaves added to N to make N tree-based; 4. vertices in N absent from a covering subtree of N ;5. covering subtrees of N such that every vertex in N is present in at least one of the trees; 6. edges (and subsequent edge subdivisions) deleted from N to make N tree-based. By definition, a given network is tree-based if and only if an optimal solution for Problem 2.3.1 to Prob-lem 2.3.4 and Problem 2.3.5 has objective function value zero and one, respectively. Moreover, Problem 2.3.1 to Problem 2.3.3 are equivalent and can be solved in Θ(|E(N )|) time [8, 10 ]. Problem 2.3.4 can be solved in 

## O(|V (N )|2|E(N )|) time [4]. Interestingly, the authors solve Problem 2.3.4 by studying Problem 2.3.2 under the additional constraints that vertex disjoint paths need to have their endpoint in a leaf. For n leaves, this construction transforms the minimization problem Problem 2.3.2 into a feasibility problem, asking for the existence of a partition of V (N ) into vertex disjoint paths with their endpoints in a leaf. Then, the authors model this question as a flow-feasibility problem which they solve by applying the max-flow-min-cut theorem. This approach can be extended to solve Problem 2.3.5 in O(|V (N )|2|E(N )| log |V (N )|) time [23 ]. To the best of our knowledge the proof of the last result is part of a master thesis which is neither publicly accessible nor available in English. We did not find any alternative source for the same result. Therefore, for the sake of completion, we include independent proofs of the results in [23 ] in Section A. We believe that our proofs are identical or very similar to the inaccessible authors’ original. In addition, for rooted not-necessarily binary tree-based networks, there are algorithms to count the number of support trees in O(|E(N )|3/2) time [17 ]. For rooted almost-binary tree-based networks, one can count and enumerate all support trees of N in O(|E(N )|) time and in O(|E(N )|) time delay, respectively [10 ]. Lastly, Problem 2.3.6 is an open problem even if constrained to selected edges whose subsequent removal transforms N into a tree-based network and who, at the time of removal, are not reticulation edges [22 ]. Moreover, the authors showed that the optimal objective function values of Problem 2.3.3 and Problem 2.3.6 are incomparable. We denote the objective function of Problem 2.3.3, Problem 2.3.4 and Problem 2.3.5 by δ∗(N ), η∗(N )

## and κ∗(N ), respectively. In addition, for a covering subtree T of N , we denote the number of vertices in N

## absent from T by η(N , T ). We call a covering subtree T of N maximum if η(N , T ) = η∗(N ). We call δ∗(N ) the 

## rooted leaf-addition tree-basedness proximity measure (ATBP), η∗(N ) the rooted covering subtree tree-basedness proximity measure (CTBP) and κ∗(N ) the rooted vertex covering tree-basedness proximity measure (VTBP). For a rooted phylogenetic network N and W ⊆ V (N ), we define ∆W = {v ∈ V (N ) : ∃ (w, v) ∈ E(N ) with w ∈ W }.Then, δ∗(N ) is a supermodular maximization problem: 3Proposition 2.4. In (B1), (B2), (C1) and (C2) the graphs on the left and right are obtained by a rNNI on (u, v) for the graph in the middle and vice versa by maintaining the direction of (u, v) and reversing it, respectively. 

## 41. there exist pairwise distinct vertices b and c incident to vertices u and v, respectively, such that the existence and direction of edges on {b, u}, {c, v} is preserved; 2. the in- and outdegrees of u and v remain at most two; 3. the acyclicity of N is preserved. Furthermore, whenever there is a degree of freedom for the direction of the edge on {u, v} after applying a rNNI on (u, v), there exist two distinct rNNIs: one which maintains edge (u, v) and one which reverses its direction. For example, the two rNNIs on (u, v) shown in Figures 1(B1) and (B2) only differ in the choice of maintaining edge (u, v) or reversing its direction. This distinction in rNNIs on (u, v) generates symmetries because internal vertices of a phylogenetic network are not labeled. Furthermore, in Figures 1(B1) and (B2) property (1) of the rNNI on (u, v) is satisfied by edges (b, u) and (v, c). In contrast, Figure 1(C1) and (C2) shows two rNNIs on (u, v) which satisfy property (1) for edges (a, u) and (v, d). Hence, while we keep reusing vertices named a, b, c, d, the role of vertices b and c in property (1) is particular and not linked to our naming conventions in later proofs. Notice that the graphs in (B1) and (B2) are equivalent to the graphs in (C2) and (C1), respectively, up to the relabeling of vertices u and v. This means, also the choice of edges in property (1) generates symmetries. Their direction plays a role, too. Specifically, in the literature a rNNI on 

## (u, v) which does not change the in- and outdegree of all vertices incident to u or v is also called a distance-1 head (tail) move if at least one of the edges on {b, u} and {c, v} has its head (tail) in {u, v} [13 ]. This means rNNIs are a proper generalization of distance-1 head and tail moves in which we allow a change of the in- and outdegree for vertices incident to u and v who do not satisfy property (1) of the rNNI on (u, v).We write either σ = e1 →H e2 or σ = e1 →T e2 if u or v is the head or tail of e1 in N , respectively, and 

## e1 satisfies property (1) of the rNNI on (u, v) while e2 does not. Similarly, we denote by either σ = e1 ⟲H e2

## or σ = e1 ⟲T e2 the rNNI operation which functions like e1 →H e2 or e1 →T e2, respectively, except that the direction on {u, v} in σ(N ) is flipped. For example, for N in the middle and bottom of Figure 1, we obtain the phylogenetic network σ(N ) in 

## (B1) for σ = ( b, u) →H (v, d) = ( v, c) →T (a, u);

## (B2) for σ = ( b, u) ⟲H (v, d) = ( v, c) ⟲T (a, u);

## (C1) for σ = ( a, u) →H (v, c) = ( v, d) →T (b, u);

## (C2) for σ = ( a, u) ⟲H (v, c) = ( v, d) ⟲T (b, u).Since reversing the direction on {u, v} produces the aforementioned symmetries, we can obtain σ(N ) = σ′(N )

## for pairwise distinct rNNI operations σ, σ′. For example, for σ = ( b, u) →H (v, d) and σ′ = ( a, u) ⟲H (v, c). A rNNI operation σ is well-defined as long as the acylicity of σ(N ) is ensured, as detailed in Lemma 1 in [9].We will not make use of this lemma because we will consider acyclicity as an ancillary condition throughout the article. We denote the number of rNNI operations to transform N ∈ N into a tree-based network N ′ ∈ NTB by 

## drNNI (N , N ′). Then, drNNI (N , N ′) is well-defined [7]. Moreover, we define the central problem of this article, a tree-basedness proximity measure based on rNNI operations: 

## Problem 2.9. Let N ∈ N . Then we call 

## δrNNI (N ) = min drNNI (N , N ′) : N ′ ∈ NTB 

## the rNNI tree-basedness proximity measure (NTBP) of N .

# 3 Combinatorial relationships between the NTBP and other proximity measures of tree-basedness 

## In this section we study the new NTBP by comparing it to the ATBP and CTBP to prove the following variation of Corollary 2.8: 

## Theorem 3.1. Let N ∈ N . Then, κ∗(N ) − 1 ≤ δ∗(N ) ≤ δrNNI (N ) ≤ η∗(N ).

## In addition, we show that the NTBP is both pairwise distinct and independent from the ATBP and CTBP .Moreover, we apply rNNI operations to characterize the ATBP , describe the CTBP and solve the NTBP exactly. 53.1 A characterization of optimal solutions to the ATBP 

## First, we characterize the ATBP of a rooted binary phylogenetic network by necessary and sufficient conditions on rNNI operations. To this end, we broaden the notion of M-W-pairs in a rooted binary phylogenetic network N .Let Z and Z′ be a M-fence and a W-fence in Z(N ), respectively. Recall that (Z, Z′) is a M-W-pair in N if there exist vertex v ∈ V (Z) ∩ V (Z′) and edges (u, v) ∈ E(Z), (v, w) ∈ E(Z′). We call v the connecting vertex of (Z, Z′).Then, for some N-fence or crown Y ∈ Z(N ), we call (Z, Z′) a• distance-1 M-W-pair in N if there exists an edge (v1, v2) ∈ E(Y ) such that v1 ∈ V (Z), v2 ∈ V (Z′) and there exists no directed path from v1 to v2 of length larger than one in N ;• distance-1 W-M-pair in N if there exists an edge (v1, v2) ∈ E(Y ) such that v1 ∈ V (Z′) and v2 ∈ V (Z);• ∨-sibling M-W-pair if there exist edges (v1, v3), (v2, v3) ∈ E(Y ) such that v1 ∈ V (Z), v2 ∈ V (Z′) and there exists no directed path from v1 to v2;• ∧-sibling M-W-pair if there exist edges (v3, v1), (v3, v2) ∈ E(Y ) such that v1 ∈ V (Z), v2 ∈ V (Z′) and there exists no directed path from v1 to v2.Observe that the non-existence of a directed path from v1 to v2 in the definition of a distance-1 W-M-pair is ensured by the degree constraints in N and therefore omitted from the definition. We call the edge defining a distance-1 M-W-pair or W-M-pair (Z, Z′) the connecting edge of (Z, Z′).

We say a M-W-rNNI-matching S in N is WN -saturated if 

## |S| = |WN |. Then, we draw the following conclusion from Theorem 3.2: 

## Corollary 3.3. Let N ∈ N . Then, δ∗(N ) ≤ δrNNI (N ). (N ) . . . )) for all i ∈ { 1, . . . , k};2. there exists a WNi -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in N i for all i ∈ { 1, . . . , k}.

## Example 3.6. Consider the networks N1 and N2 on the left and right in Figure 5, respectively. Hence, the number of yellow vertices η∗(N1) can be made arbitrarily large while δrNNI (N1) = 1 holds. Lemma 3.7 highlights a central issue when studying the CTBP for N ∈ N : covering subtrees are a genuine global substructure of the network while rNNI operations are local. Lemma 3.7.1 was derived from the maximality of the covering subtree T . Example 3.6 is an application of this characterization. However, the upper bound on the CTBP of σ(N ) in Lemma 3.7.2 can be arbitrarily large because we cannot derive a sufficient condition for the maximality of covering subtrees in σ(N ) from rNNI operation σ alone. This means, we need structural constraints on the neighborhood of edges affected by a rNNI operation to quantify the relationship between the CTBP and NTBP further. ## Proposition 3.8. Let N ∈ N . If N is not tree-based, then there exists a rNNI operation σ such that η∗(σ(N )) = 

## η∗(N ) − 1.Proof. Assume N is not tree-based. and let T ∗ be shown in red in Figure 7. First, assume (u, v) ∈ E(N )

## η(σ(N ), Tσ) = η∗(N ) − 1. Since the paths P(v, c) and P(v, d) in N are not in T ∗, the maximality of T ∗ implies that Tσ is a maximum covering subtree of σ(N ). Thus, η∗(σ(N )) = η∗(N ) − 1. Next, assume (u, v) ∈ E(N ), dout (v) = 1. Then, the edges incident to (u, v) are shown in the graph on the left in Figure 7(B). Let σ = ( c, v) ⟲H (b, u). Since P(c, d) is not a subpath of T ∗, we can apply Lemma 3.7.2 for reversed roles of N and σ(N ) to obtain η∗(N ) = η∗(σ(N )) + 1. The remaining cases shown in Figure 7(C) and (D) are analogous to Figure 7(B) and (A), respectively. Observe that the relationship between the NTBP and CTBP described by Proposition 3.8 is significantly simpler than the necessary and sufficient conditions in Theorem 3.2 to characterize the relationship between the NTBP and ATBP . Moreover, while there exists no rNNI operation σ such that δ∗(σ(N )) ≤ δ∗(N ) − 2, Lemma 3.7 tells us that η∗(σ(N )) ≤ η∗(N ) − k is possible for any integer k ≥ 2. This qualitative difference between the ATBP and CTBP relative to the NTBP stems in part from the fact that a maximum covering subtree of a rooted binary phylogenetic network is not unique while the set of maximal W-fences is unique (see Theorem 2.1). Now, in light of Theorem 2.7, an immediate consequence of Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.8 is the following: 

## Corollary 3.9. Let N ∈ N . Then, δ∗(N ) ≤ δrNNI (N ) ≤ η∗(N ). Both inequalities hold with equality if and only if there exists a WN -saturated M-W-matching in N .

## Proof. First, let k be a positive integer and let N ∈ N such that there exists a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in N for which Theorem 3.2.2 is satisfied at least once. This means, there exists a distance-1 M-W-pair 

## (Y, Z) such that its connecting edge (u, v) is incident to the endpoint of Z. Choose N such that u is the endpoint of Y and (u, v) is not in a W-fence in Z(N ). Then, there exist a, b ∈ V (N ), a̸ = v, b̸ = u, such that 

## (u, a), (u, v), (b, v) ∈ E(N ). The graph on the left in Figure 8 depicts Y and Z in blue and red, respectively. Then, we consider the rNNI operation σ = ( v, c) →T (u, a) in the same figure. Now, we show how N can be modified to achieve η∗(σ(N )) = η∗(N ) − k. Afterwards we will modify N further to maintain the existence of a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in N .

## Case 1: There exists a maximum covering subtree T ∗ of N such that (u, a) ∈ E(T ∗) and (u, v), (b, v) /∈ E(T ∗).Let v′ ∈ V (T ∗), v′̸ = u, such that there exists a directed path P(v′, v) with E(P(v′, v)) ⊂ E(N ) \ E(T ∗).Necessarily b ∈ P(v′, v) because u ∈ V (T ∗). Then, there exists a covering subtree Tσ of σ(N ) we obtain from T ∗ by 1. removing the maximal length subpath P of T ∗ with endpoint u consisting only of edge subdivisions of T ∗;2. adding P(v′, v) by subdividing its last edge by u (see Figure 8 for last edge (b, v)). Let p = |V (T ∗) \ V (Tσ)| and q = |V (Tσ) \ V (T ∗)| = |V (P(v′, v)) | − 2. Then, we have 

## η(σ(N ), Tσ) = η(N , T ∗) + p − q.If k = q − p, then η∗(σ(N )) = η(σ(N ), Tσ) = η∗(N ) − k follows from the maximality of T ∗. We show how N can be modified to draw the same conclusion for k̸ = q − p. Without loss of generality k > q − p.Otherwise we reverse the role of paths P(v′, v) and P in the following. Then, for a positive integer m, we replace an internal vertex of P(v′, v), say vertex b, in N by the auxiliary graph Hm(b) shown in Figure 9. Subsequently, T ∗ might no longer be maximal. In this case the red and /or blue paths in Figure 9 are subpaths of a maximum covering subtree T ′ of N with maximal overlap |V (T ′) ∩ V (T ∗)|.If the blue path is in T ′ but not the red path, then we replace T ∗ by T ′ and all previous arguments for 

## T ∗ still apply. Indeed, again (b, v), (v, c) /∈ E(T ∗), p cannot increase and q is a function q(m) increasing in m. This means, we can prove our claim by choosing q(m) = k + p for a sufficiently large m.If the red path is in T ′, then T ′ also contains the blue path by the maximality of T ′. Now, (b, v), (v, c) ∈

## E(T ′) because T ′ and N have the same leafset. Then, there exists a directed subpath P(v, c′) of 

## T ′ of minimal length such that c′ ∈ V (T ′) ∩ V (T ∗). For a positive integer m′, we replace parent 

## w ∈ V (T ∗) \ V (T ′) of c′ in N by auxiliary graph Hm′ . By choosing m′ sufficiently large we can ensure that 

## T ′ is no longer a maximum covering subtree of N . Hence, no maximum covering subtree of N contains the red path of Hm and we can return back to our previous case to consider T ∗ as a maximal covering subtree of N which contains the blue path but not the red path. 

## Case 2: There exists a maximum covering subtree T ∗ of N such that (u, v) ∈ E(T ∗) and (b, v) /∈ E(T ∗).Analogous to Case 1 because (b, v) /∈ E(T ∗) and (v, c) ∈ E(T ∗).

## Case 3: There exists a maximum covering subtree T ∗ of N such that (b, v) ∈ E(T ∗). Analogous to Case 1 or 2 if (u, a) /∈ E(T ∗) by reversing the direction on all arguments. Hence, assume (u, a) ∈ E(T ∗). Then, 

## (d, c) ∈ E(N ) \ E(T ∗) for a vertex d̸ = v. Subdivide edges (b, v) and (d, c) by vertices x and y, and add edge (x, y) to N . Then, path P(b, c) in T ∗ can be replaced by the path constituted by edges (b, x), (x, y),

## Case 4: There exists a maximum covering subtree T ∗ of N such that (u, a), (u, v), (b, v) /∈ E(T ∗). Then, for a positive integer m, replace b in N by the auxiliary graph Hm(b). Finally, observe that there does not exist a Wσ(N )-saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in σ(N ) only if the insertion of auxiliary graph Hm(b) or edge (x, y) in Case 3 does change any of conditions in Theorem 3.2.1 to Theorem 3.2.5 satisfied by the original network. ## containing b as an internal vertex is decomposed into two N-fences through the insertion of Hm(b) (see Figure 9). Otherwise b is a tree vertex. Then, we insert the edges and vertices shown in bold in Figure 10(A) into Hm(b). This means, b is the endpoint of a M-fence A (shown in blue) and either v or w is an internal vertex of a W-fence B (shown in red). Indeed, if v and w are in a W-fence in Z(N ), then (u, v) is in a W-fence, contradicting our initial choice of N . This means, (A, B) is either a M-W-pair or a distance-1 M-W-pair such that its connecting edge is incident to the endpoint of B, ensuring the existence of a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching. Next, consider the insertion of edge (x, y) in Case 3. In case (C) the existence of a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching is guaranteed, too. To see this consider the effect of the rNNI operation shown in Figure 10(C) on W-fences. ## and therefore |Bk(N )| ≤ | B1(N )|k ≤ (3m + r)k.Notice that the construction of Bk(N ) in Algorithm 1 allows us to backtrack in line 6 to also identify a sequence of k networks ˆ N1, . . . , ˆ Nk ∈ N such that ˆ N1 = N , ˆ Nk ∈ NTB and ˆ Ni ∈ B1( ˆNi−1) for all i ∈ { 2, . . . , k}.However, since η∗(N ) ≤ 2r − 2 (Lemma 5.20 in [13 ]), the runtime guarantee of Proposition 3.13 is exponential in the number of reticulation vertices. This means, only if r grows logarithmic in the input length, i.e., for a family of input networks which is close to tree-based, then Algorithm 1 solves the NTBP exactly in polynomial time. In the special case that there exists a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in N (Corollary 3.3) we can strengthen this result because then the NTBP of N can be solved exactly in linear time [10 ].15 4 Conclusion and future research 

## In this article we have conducted a comparative study of the δrNNI to derive Theorem 3.1, a linear order of all known proximity measures for tree-basedness of rooted binary phylogenetic networks. The same result might hold if we remove the restriction to binary networks because our proof rests on Theorem 2.1 which has been extended to the non-binary case [18 ]. However, this extended decomposition of a rooted phylogenetic network into maximal zig-zag trails is characterised by three forbidden subgraphs and the differentiation of crowns into five pairwise distinct types of maximal zig-zag paths (see Figure 3 in [18 ]). Therefore, a generalization of Theorem 3.2 to rooted non-binary phylogenetic networks might be achievable when working with the extended maximal zig-zag trail decomposition. Though we think a substantially longer proof and possibly proof automation are necessary. We also notice that the application of Theorem 3.1 leads to a combinatorial explosion of candidates for an optimal solution to δrNNI (see Corollary 3.3 and Example 3.4). This complicates a potential characterization of a family of networks in N for which δ∗(N ) = δrNNI (N ) holds. The same challenge persists in the construction of networks in N for which rNNI moves tighten neither lower bounds δ∗(N ) nor upper bounds η∗(N ) particularly well. Specifically, for any positive integers k1, k2, we have shown that there exists a family F of networks N ∈ N such that δ∗(N ) + k1 = δrNNI (N ) = η∗(N ) − k2 by first applying Proposition 3.5 and then Proposition 3.10. Here the lack of uniqueness of maximum covering subtrees affected by a rNNI operation (see Lemma 3.7) in contrast to the effect of rNNI operations on W-fences (see Theorem 3.2) differentiates the claim of Proposition 3.5 for all networks in N from the network existence claim in Proposition 3.10. Similar to the question on generalizing Theorem 3.2 from binary to non-binary networks, the construction of N ∈ N in the proof of Proposition 3.10 might still be possible for any given 

## WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching with a substantially longer proof. While the complexity of the NTBP is an open question, we know from Proposition 3.13 that for a sufficiently small k2 we can compute δrNNI in polynomial time because η∗(N ) can be computed efficiently. Hence, for sufficiently large k1 and k2, family F

## seems to contain the input networks for which the NTBP might be hard to solve. Further future research directions concern the boundaries of our study. For example, one can consider the NNI proximity measure of tree-basedness for unrooted instead of rooted phylogenetic networks, whose decision version is NP-complete [6] to further study its relation with comparable proximity measures. Furthermore, one can consider more general topological rearrangement operations than rNNI such as Subnet Prune and Regraft (SNPR) operations [2] to study proximity from tree-basedness in rooted phylogenetic networks. This generalization is not trivial as SNPR operations can reconnect vertices at large topological distances, allowing for large distances in M-W-pairs or W-M-pairs to describe or characterize the ATBP through SNPR moves while ensuring acyclicity of the network. This leads to more relevant subgraphs in an analysis of SNPR moves similar to Theorem 3.2. Lastly, one can define a rNNI proximity measure from orchard networks, a subclass of tree-based networks, or tree-child networks, a subclass of orchard networks [15 ]. To the best of our knowledge both measures have not been studied before and might be interesting because the analogous version of the related ATBP for orchard or tree-child network is NP-hard and linear-time solvable, respectively [21 ]. This question also includes the study of new upper bounds because the CTBP is derived from the definition of tree-basedness. For example, one could study the minimum number of vertices in a network who do not have a tree vertex as their child as a proximity measure for tree-childness to maybe obtain upper bounds on the rNNI tree-childness proximity measure.

## Proposition 3.5. For any integers k > 0 and any N ∈ N for which there exists a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching, there exists N ′ ∈ N such that WN ′ = WN , MN ′ = MN and δ∗(N ′) + k = δrNNI (N ′).Proof. Assume there exists a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in N for which one of Theorem 3.2.1 to Theo-rem 3.2.5 is satisfied at least once. We proved our claim for the condition in Theorem 3.2.1. Conditions in Theorem 3.2.2 to Theorem 3.2.5 are illustrated in the graphs on the left in Figure 12 (from top to bottom in order of the conditions) by associating red vertices and edges to the W-fence Z and blue vertices and edges to the M-fence Z′ satisfying the respective conditions. Then, the graphs in the middle depict the (possibly repeated) insertion of a few vertices and edges which increase the minimal topological distance between any pair of vertices x ∈ Z, y ∈ Z′. Observe that this construction transforms N into N ′ ∈ N with WN ′ = WN and 

## MN ′ = MN such that Z and Z′ no longer satisfy any one of the conditions in Theorem 3.2. However, applying the rNNI operation σ shown in Figure 12 to N ′ yields the graph on the right in the same figure. In each case we can identify a W-fence and a M-fence in Z(σ(N ′)) (drawn in red and blue, respectively) which satisfy the same condition in Theorem 3.2 as our initial zig-zag paths Z and Z′ in Z(N ). Furthermore, by construction σ does not increase |WN ′ | or |MN ′ |. This means, there exists a Wσ(N ′ )-saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in σ(N ′) because there exists a WN -saturated M-W-rNNI-matching in N . Thus, Corollary 3.3 implies δ∗(N ′) + 1 = δrNNI (N ′) and we can draw the same conclusion as in the case of Theorem 3.2.1. 19 .
